reference.source: Sherlock's Diseases of the Liver and Biliary System / Suchy Liver Disease in Children
clinicalPearls: An autosomal recessive cholestatic disorder caused by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in TJP2, encoding tight junction protein 2
Presents in infancy with cholestasis, pruritus, jaundice, and fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption
Characteristically has a low or normal serum gamma-glutamyl transferase, like PFIC types 1 and 2
Coagulopathy from vitamin K deficiency can be an early and dangerous manifestation
TJP2 maintains the integrity of the hepatocyte tight junction at the bile canaliculus, so its loss allows bile to leak and injure hepatocytes
There is an associated risk of hepatocellular carcinoma, warranting long-term surveillance
Management is supportive with ursodeoxycholic acid, fat-soluble vitamins, antipruritic measures, biliary diversion in selected cases, and liver transplantation for progressive disease
reference.pathophysiology: PFIC type 4 is caused by biallelic mutations in TJP2, which encodes a scaffolding protein of the hepatocyte tight junction that seals the bile canaliculus. Loss of functional TJP2 disrupts the paracellular barrier between hepatocytes, allowing concentrated bile to regurgitate into the hepatocyte and paracellular space, causing cholestasis and progressive hepatocellular injury. The gamma-glutamyl transferase remains low or normal because canalicular membrane enzymes are not shed as in obstructive cholestasis. Chronic injury may progress to fibrosis and cirrhosis, and there is an increased risk of hepatocellular carcinoma.
additionalInvestigations: Serum bile acids and gamma-glutamyl transferase (characteristically low/normal GGT)
Liver function tests and fractionated bilirubin
Coagulation profile and fat-soluble vitamin levels
Liver biopsy with immunostaining for TJP2 and assessment of fibrosis
Genetic testing of TJP2 and the wider PFIC gene panel
Alpha-fetoprotein and imaging for hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance
redFlags: Vitamin K-dependent coagulopathy with intracranial or other bleeding
Progression to cirrhosis with portal hypertension
Intractable pruritus with severe impairment of quality of life
reference.prognosis: The course is variable, ranging from milder cholestasis to progressive liver disease requiring transplantation; the increased risk of hepatocellular carcinoma means lifelong surveillance is important even when liver function appears preserved.
pitfalls: Assuming a normal GGT excludes significant inherited cholestasis
Failing to institute hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance
Overlooking vitamin K deficiency as a cause of bleeding in infancy
Not recognising the disorder within the broader PFIC differential when genotype is unknown
